entries.title: A HRW report shows how South Korean women face systemic barriers to climbing the career ladder
entries.summary: A new report shows how in South Korea, women on average earn less and have fewer employment opportunities throughout their lives.
entries.content:
September 26, 2026

A new report shows how in South Korea, women on average earn less and have fewer employment opportunities throughout their lives.

At 27, a woman in South Korea earns 8% less than male peers. By her late 50s, she earns 50% less. This is according to government wage data published in a recent Human Rights Watch (HRW) report.  

South Korea is a global technology and industrial powerhouse, but its gender pay gap has remained the highest in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) since comparable records began in 1992.

"The gender division of labor inside the home leads directly to a gender division of labor in the labor market," Min Hee Kim, a Korean activist for women labor struggles, told DW.

The problem, she argues, is not simply that women are paid less than men. As women age, the kinds of work available to them narrows and the consequences of lower pay, career breaks and precarious jobs accumulate.  

For the report, "Too Old and a Woman," HRW interviewed 41 South Korean women aged 28 to 87 about their working lives.  

Structural barriers to women's careers

Discrimination has changed form rather than disappeared, Kim said. Until the 1980s, it was legal for employers to fire women simply for getting married, a practice known as "marriage-based dismissal," where employers assumed a married woman would soon leave to raise children anyway. 

Today, "it is difficult to openly say, 'We won't hire you because you're a woman,'" Kim added. But caregiving responsibilities still fall on women, pushing them into lower-paid jobs when they try to return to work. 

According to the HRW report, women's university attainment has passed men's since the 1980s. Higher education would suggest equal opportunity after graduation, but the job market says otherwise.

One year after graduating, women already earn 22% less than men, according to a 2024 study.

Many women told HRW that after leaving work for marriage or children, chances of returning to the workforce were limited to a handful of jobs such as call centers, cleaning or caregiving.

Women who opt to focus on their career told HRW they hit a glass ceiling at work. Women held 18% of manager jobs in 2024, and only five of 38 senior civil servants were women.

Wages peak and drop off

Women's wages peak in their late 30s and then steadily decline, according to Labor Ministry survey data cited by HRW.

South Korea's Gender Ministry told HRW that career interruptions, along with occupational segregation and discrimination within organizations, drive the gap.

J. Mi-sook, 53, told HRW that her three years of experience weren't recognized by her next employer, so she started at entry level on a lower salary.

The longer women spend outside the workforce, the less experience they accumulate on their resumes, which results in less pay and less work stability.

Kim pointed to structural discrimination, a concept from the report that HRW describes as discrimination so embedded in social practices and institutions that even the people harmed by it may not recognize it as a problem.  

"When you are alone, it is easy to think, 'It's because I'm not capable enough,' or 'It's because I'm getting older,'" she said. It's only when women who've had similar experiences meet and talk, she added, that they realize, "this wasn't just my problem."

It gets harder as you get older

Park Jae-soon, 61, was forced to retire at 60 from a utility company and now works part-time as a care worker. Her annual income fell from 55 million won ($40,500/€35,600) to 15.6 million won, a 72% drop.

HRW argues the mandatory retirement age and the "peak wage" system, which lets employers cut older workers' pay in the years before retirement, should both be abolished.

According to data cited in the report, women received 53% of men's National Old Age Pension on average in October 2025, a 47% gap.

"I think what is important here is that this is not simply a problem of middle-aged women having difficulty finding jobs," Kim said.

"The work that women have traditionally done inside the home, like cleaning, cooking, caregiving and managing other people's emotions, is classified as 'work suitable for women' when it enters the labor market, and then low wages are assigned to it," she added.

From first paycheck to pension

HRW argues the disadvantage builds stage by stage, from a woman's first paycheck up until her pension.

"Career interruption among women in their 30s is already a pension issue," Kim said. "Part-time work among women in their 40s is a pension issue, and low wages among women in their 50s are already a pension issue," she added.

South Korea's government has said it will pursue a phased increase in the statutory retirement age from 60 to 65.

"This cannot be solved with just one policy. Equal pay for equal work needs to be actually implemented, wage structures need to be transparent, and care needs to be treated as a public responsibility rather than something that is pushed onto individual families and women," Kim said.

The rights activist said the report is an important starting point, but believes its picture is incomplete.

Most interviewees were recruited through civic organizations and largely in Seoul, she noted, while disabled women, migrant workers and others may experience a different combination of age and gender discrimination.

"The important question is not simply, 'How much discrimination do women face?'" she said. "It is which women, in what positions, become increasingly distanced from which resources and rights as they grow older."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Deadly blast rips through Athens building, near Acropolis
entries.summary: Several foreign tourists remain missing after an explosion brought down a building in Athens' tourist area of Plaka, with the city's mayor calling it an "incredible disaster."
entries.content:
Greece

Deadly blast rips through Athens building, near Acropolis

September 26, 2026

Several foreign tourists remain missing after an explosion brought down a building in Athens' tourist area of Plaka, with the city's mayor calling it an "incredible disaster."

Rescuers have recovered the body of a young woman following a building collapse in Plaka, in central Athens, a Greek fire brigade official said Saturday.

Later, Greek public broadcaster ERT said a man's body was also recovered from the rubble.

The building was brought down by a large blast which injured three other people and damaged shops and cars near the site.

"The damage extends along the entire street as well as the street behind the building," said Athens Mayor Haris Doukas. "We are talking about an incredible disaster."

Several people, believed to be foreign nationals, remain missing.

On Saturday, Greek news agency ANA reported that the female victim whose body was retrieved was an American tourist, sharing the holiday rental with her husband and another couple.

Cause of the blast still uncertain

Authorities suspect a gas leak caused the Friday blast, but the sequence of events was not immediately clear.

"Something went terribly wrong," Doukas said.

Local media reported the missing people included a Briton and a Greek woman who lived on the second floor, and four American tourists staying on the first floor.

While their nationalities have not been officially confirmed, a police official said the group of tourists had been expected to check in for a flight from Athens on early Friday afternoon.

Excavators on the scene

Rescuers were using sniffer dogs and thermal cameras to search for possible survivors. According to ANA, dozens of firefighters and six vehicles have been deployed to help with the search, including two specialized rescue vehicles.

Excavators were also deployed to clear the rubble, according to photos from the scene.

Plaka is close to many Athens most visited sites, including the Acropolis and the Temple of Zeus.

entries.title: Germany news: EU ministers meet for migration showdown
entries.summary: European interior ministers hold migration talks in Munich as the bloc plans to strengthen borders and speed up deportations. Also, will Cologne or Munich win the battle to bid for the Olympic Games? DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: EU ministers meet for migration showdown

Published September 26, 2026last updated September 26, 2026

European interior ministers hold migration talks in Munich as the bloc plans to strengthen borders and speed up deportations. Also, will Cologne or Munich win the battle to bid for the Olympic Games? DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • European interior ministers gather in Munich to tighten EU migration policy
  • Germany's Olympic committee to decide which city will bid to host the Games in 2036, 2040 or 2044
  • Trade unions stage protests in 15 cities against health, welfare cuts
  • Former Chancellor Angela Merkel, a Protestant, wins top Catholic charity's prize

Follow our blog for the latest news and analysis from across Germany for the weekend of September 26-27, 2026.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Rail services canceled, delayed after suspected cable theft

Rail services canceled, delayed after suspected cable theft

Police blamed disruption to high-speed rail services in western Germany on deliberate damage to signal cabling overnight.

National rail operator Deutsche Bahn said trains running between Dortmund and Munich, Hamburg and Basel, and northern Germany and Cologne faced cancellations, delays and diversions.

According to the Zuginfo.nrw website, the entire Gelsenkirchen metropolitan area is currently impassable.

A police spokesman said officers were investigating suspected cable theft on a railway line in Gelsenkirchen-Ückendorf, where signals and control systems had failed.

The suspects are believed to have crudely cut and ripped out cables beside the tracks at several points.

It is unclear how long the repair work will take.

Skip next section Caritas honors Merkel with prize for social cohesion

Caritas honors Merkel with prize for social cohesion

Former Chancellor Angela Merkel, a Protestant, received one of the highest honors of the Catholic Church's social welfare charity in Germany.

The 72-year-old was awarded the Elisabeth Prize by the Catholic Caritas Association at an event in the southern city of Augsburg on Friday evening.

The prize is named after Saint Elizabeth of Thuringia, who lived from 1207 to 1231 and who helped people in need. She is the patron saint of Caritas.

The honor recognized Merkel's commitment to social cohesion, with Caritas President Eva Welskop-Deffaa paying tribute to the "inner compass with which she [Merkel] successfully steered the country's fortunes."

The former chancellor told the roughly 400 guests that "there will always be a need for people to be there for one another."

Once seen by some as Mutti — Germany’s reassuring mother figure — Merkel has become an increasingly divisive figure because of her 2015 decision to open the borders to more than a million refugees.

Critics say Merkel’s decision fueled years of backlash that helped turn the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from a fringe protest party into a force that now leads most national polls.

Skip next section Dobrindt seeks 'hardening' of EU borders at Munich talks

Dobrindt seeks 'hardening' of EU borders at Munich talks

Several European Union interior ministers are meeting in Munich this afternoon to discuss tightening the bloc's migration policy.

A spokesperson for German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Münchner Merkur newspaper that the talks will focus on the "implementation of a shift in migration policy."

The 17 ministers will discuss "further refining the European Migration Pact, consistently hardening the European Union's external borders, and accelerating returns from Europe," the spokesperson added.

Germany and Denmark, Austria, the Netherlands, and Greece are due to hold separate talks about the creation of deportation centers or return hubs in third countries.

Germany hopes to secure a deal with a country in Africa or possibly Asia by the end of the year.

Dobrindt's spokesperson said the EU's border agency, Frontex, could be turned into a "border protection and genuine return agency."

Currently, EU member states are responsible for returning asylum seekers whose applications have failed.

EU Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner will also attend the Munich talks.

Skip next section Munich or Cologne: Germany set to pick Olympic bid city

Munich or Cologne: Germany set to pick Olympic bid city

Germany's Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) will reveal at lunchtime which city will bid to host a future Olympic Games.

After the capital, Berlin, withdrew earlier this week, the vote will be a two-horse race  between Munich and Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr to be the candidate city for either the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Games.

Germany is keeping its options open regarding which Games to bid for, as the 2036 Olympics is widely expected to go to an Asian country.

The year 2036 is also politically sensitive as it would mark 100 years since Berlin hosted the 1936 Olympics during the Nazi era.

Some policymakers want Germany to bid for 2040, as it will mark 50 years since German reunification.

If it wins, Munich plans to host most Olympic events within city limits and already has stadia and other sports infrastructure in place, including the Olympic Park, which was built for the 1972 Games.

Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr plans to spread the Games across several cities, including Schalke for swimming events, Düsseldorf for basketball and football at Borussia Dortmund's 81,000-seat stadium.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from DW. In Munich, you'll often hear Grüss Gott (greet God), while in Cologne and Germany's Rhine-Ruhr region, people often say Tachchen (Hey there).

It's decision day for both cities as Germany's Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) picks which one will bid to host the Olympic Games in 2036, 2040, or 2044.

Munich will also be hosting European interior ministers for talks on implementing a tougher EU migration policy.

Fifteen other cities, including Berlin, Hamburg and Nuremberg, will stage protests against the government's planned cuts to the social welfare bill.

We'll bring you updates on these and other top news stories from across Germany throughout the day.

entries.title: India news: New Delhi, Islamabad trade accusations at UN General Assembly
entries.summary: Shehbaz Sharif criticized India's policy on Kashmir and praised Pakistan's military, while New Delhi accused Islamabad of supporting cross-border terrorism. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India, Pakistan trade accusations at UN General Assembly

Published September 26, 2026last updated September 26, 2026

Shehbaz Sharif criticized India's policy on Kashmir and praised Pakistan's military, while New Delhi accused Islamabad of supporting cross-border terrorism. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • India and Pakistan traded accusations at the UN General Assembly (UNGA)
  • Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for "a just and fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute" and accused New Delhi of "weaponizing" water
  • India accused Islamabad of "terrorism, deceit and duplicity"
  • Protests across New Delhi call for women's safety yet again

Here are some of the major headlines from India on Saturday, September 26:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Jammu and Kashmir assembly seeks restoration of statehood, BJP protests

Jammu and Kashmir assembly seeks restoration of statehood, BJP protests

Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Friday moved a resolution in the legislative assembly seeking the immediate restoration of full statehood to the region leading to chaos in the assembly, media reports said.

"We have been waiting. In public and private meetings and every forum, we made the government of India remember that you had made a promise with the people of J&K but it is not being fulfilled," Abdullah said in the assembly of the Union Territory.

Describing it as Prime Minister Narendra Modi's promise, Abdullah said that it should now be fulfilled, adding that the central government had promised to restore it after delimitation and elections.

He also cited administrative difficulties arising from J&K's status as a Union Territory.

The resolution was supported by the ruling National Conference, as well as other parties, but triggered an uproar from Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) legislators who objected to seeking greater autonomy for J&K.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP government in 2019 had revoked Kashmir's special status, known as Article 370, which had allowed Jammu and Kashmir to have its own constitution and a degree of internal autonomy.

Under locally approved laws, this meant that only local Kashmiris could vote, own land, and apply for government jobs.

A land ownership provision, called Article 35A, was also scrapped, leading to accusations of being a move by the BJP to engineer a demographic change in the Muslim-majority region.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Protests across New Delhi call for women's safety yet again

IN PICTURES: Protests across New Delhi call for women's safety yet again

Women, particularly students, have taken to the streets across New Delhi in recent days to protest recent cases of sexual violence against women and girls.

The demonstrations were prompted by the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old girl in a Delhi park, as well as reported cases of molestation involving minors in Jamui and Samastipur in the eastern state of Bihar.

Skip next section India-Pakistan tensions flare at UNGA

India-Pakistan tensions flare at UNGA

India and Pakistan traded accusations at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Friday, with Islamabad criticizing India's stance on Kashmir and New Delhi accusing Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism.

Addressing the General Assembly, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for "a just and fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute," alleging human rights violations in the region.

Sharif also brought up the military clashes last year between the uneasy neighbors, calling them "external aggression from India under a false pretext."

Pakistan considers Indian missile strikes on May 7 to be the start of the low-level conflict, which ran for less than a week, while India contends that the strikes were retaliation for an attack in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in April last year.

He added that India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance had no legal basis and accused New Delhi of "weaponizing" water.

India rejected Sharif's remarks. First Secretary at India's UN mission Petal Gahlot accused Pakistan of "terrorism, deceit and duplicity" and said Islamabad's support for cross-border terrorism would have consequences.

Gahlot also criticized Pakistan's military establishment and its treatment of minorities, while reiterating India's position that Jammu and Kashmir is an integral part of the country.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

India and Pakistan traded barbs at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, as the acrimonious neighbors used the global forum to air their long-running grievances.

Meanwhile, the Congress Party protested across several states demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumarover the Election Commission's handling of the revision of voter rolls.

For all this and more, follow our live blog.

entries.title: Thailand: Bangkok flooding triggers disaster declaration
entries.summary: Rainfall over the past three days has caused heavy flooding in the Thai capital. A state of disaster has been declared in all 50 districts in Bangkok.
entries.content:
Thailand

Thailand: Bangkok flooding triggers disaster declaration

September 26, 2026

Rainfall over the past three days has caused heavy flooding in the Thai capital. A state of disaster has been declared in all 50 districts in Bangkok.

Authorities in Bangkok on Saturday declared a disaster across 50 districts in  Thailand's capital after days of heavy rainfall caused severe flooding.

Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said the eastern parts of the city were impacted most.

By Saturday afternoon, Chadchart said the situation had "stabilized" and added: "If more rainwater doesn't fall in the area, it will be solved."

"If the rain stops, it is expected that it will take two to three days to drain the floodwater," he said in an update on social media.

Situation in brief

  • Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said the situation has "stabilized"

  • Emergency ​advisory for ⁠people living near canals to move possessions to ​higher ground

  • Bangkok city officials open shelter for evacuees

  • More rain forecast into Sunday

More rain in Bangkok forecast

Chadchart said almost 300 millimeters (11.8 inches) of rain had fallen since Thursday afternoon and warned that more rain was expected.

"The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full," the governor said on social media and advised residents to move their possessions to higher ground.

"The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled," he said.

Chadchart urged bedridden patients dependent on life-saving medical equipment to consider a temporary stay in hospital.

Thai authorities said more than 84,000 people in 21 provinces nationwide have been impacted by flooding as of Saturday, especially in the central region.

Floods evoke memories of deadly 2011 deluge

"The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now," local vendor Somkid Pheuk-ngam, told the AFP news agency.

"I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now," she told AFP, adding that while she often gets flooded, "I think this time is worse than the 2011 flood."

Flooding across Thailand in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes.

Thailand's Meteorological Department warned the heavy rain would persist in most parts of the country through Sunday and pointed to a strong low-pressure system dominating the central region and strengthening monsoon conditions.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: OpenAI tools post user images from ChatGPT online
entries.summary: OpenAI said it found 53 cases in which user-uploaded image links on ChatGPT were shared with third-party websites. The company said it had removed most of these links.
entries.content:
TechnologyGlobal issues

OpenAI tools post user images from ChatGPT online

September 26, 2026

OpenAI said it found 53 cases in which user-uploaded image links on ChatGPT were shared with third-party websites. The company said it had removed most of these links.

Artificial intelligence giant OpenAI on Friday acknowledged that its AI tools had posted images users provided to ChatGPT on online sites, without the company's knowledge, in yet another example of AI agents operating outside of their confines.

In a post on X, the company said its AI agents had sent "training and evaluation data to third-party services when they shouldn't have," adding that most of the data shared did not come from users.

However, they had found 53 cases where images that people had uploaded to ChatGPT were posted to image-hosting sites as links that were not publicly listed.

"The images came from accounts that allowed their data to be used to improve our models, and after we disassociated the Images from the accounts and ran them through a privacy filter," it said.

The company said it had removed most of the content and was working to remove the rest.

Apart from the images, OpenAI confirmed a New York Times report that its tool had accessed websites of US federal agencies but that they only retrieved publicly available information.

Rising fear of rogue AI

The latest disclosure comes amid heightened global concerns about AI systems escaping human control and hacking into external websites, as well as industry calls for a slowdown on AI development — a move which OpenAI said it supports.

Friday's post also clarified that the cases of unauthorized sharing occurred before a fresh round of safeguards were implemented over a month ago.

In July, OpenAI had said internal cybersecurity evaluations showed that its models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Friday said it was "still the most severe event we've seen."

"We are continuing to review agent activity in research and evaluation runs, working backward month by month starting from the Hugging Face incident," OpenAI said in a safety blog post on Friday, adding that it would "provide further updates" in time.

Investigation finds OpenAI agents attempting hacks

AI evaluator and research lab Transluce on Friday said that it also found that AI agents, appearing to originate from OpenAI, attempted a rudimentary hack on the US Department of Education website for the department's civil rights office. The agents did not succeed, according to the independent investigation.

The company said it found "additional rogue activities," some of which were not directly attributable to OpenAI, targeting other government agencies, including the Justice Department and the Commerce Department, as well as some state government websites in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas and New York.

entries.title: White House bars CNN from covering upcoming Trump trip, broadcaster says
entries.summary: CNN said its journalists have been barred from accompanying President Donald Trump on his upcoming trip to Tennessee. The episode marks the Trump administration's latest salvo against the major cable news network.
entries.content:
United States of America

White House bars CNN from covering upcoming Trump trip

September 26, 2026

CNN said its journalists have been barred from accompanying President Donald Trump on his upcoming trip to Tennessee. The episode marks the Trump administration's latest salvo against the major cable news network.

American news broadcaster CNN said its journalists were not allowed to board Air Force One for a planned trip with President Donald Trump on Saturday.

CNN was scheduled to travel on Air Force One to Knoxville, Tennessee, where Trump was expected to watch a college football game.

The news organization was to be the representative of the TV press pool for the weekend, meaning that it would cover the president and share video and information with the four other big networks that are part of the press pool.

CNN was replaced by Real America's Voice News, a conservative network, the Associated Press reported.

The episode represents the latest showdown between the Trump administration and media networks that the president believes to be unfavorable in their coverage.

Trump bans CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from White House

Trump earlier this week barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House after he said the networks report "fiction and lies."

Major TV networks, including DW, then cut off their pooled coverage of the president in solidarity. 

A federal judge  temporarily struck down the ban in a ruling on Thursday after the outlets filed a lawsuit.

But the order from the judge addressed "hard passes" to the White House grounds and didn't directly address pool duties.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: TikTok agrees to settle with Alabama state over teen safety
entries.summary: The settlement involves TikTok adding several child safety measures to its platform including time limits and increased parental control. It is similar to a recent settlement competitor Meta had reached.
entries.content:
September 26, 2026

The settlement involves TikTok adding several child safety measures to its platform including time limits and increased parental control. It is similar to a recent settlement competitor Meta had reached.

Short-form content sharing platform TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance reached a settlement with Alabama, the southeastern US state said on Friday, days ahead of what would have been a revealing trial over teen safety and its impact on their mental health.

As part of the deal, TikTok agreed to pay $100 million (€87.7 million) to the state of Alabama and enact measures for teens including a two-hour daily use limit, restricted access for children and pauses after 15 minutes of use.

However, the payout could rise to $300 million if 40 other states sign similar agreements with the company within a stipulated time period, the document said.

What have TikTok and Alabama state said after the settlement?

"This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually ​enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens," a spokesperson for TikTok's US operations said in a statement.

Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall sued the social media giant last year.

At least 27 other states and Washington DC have brought similar lawsuits. Apart from these, TikTok faces thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts and municipalities over its impact on teen mental health. Meta Platforms, Snap Inc and Alphabet's YouTube are also defendants in many of these ​cases.

"This is a great day for Alabama parents. Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction. TikTok has agreed to give parents real control over what their kids see and how much time they spend on the app," Marshall said in a press release.

With this, the company has settled all cases selected for trial against it, including claims by five young people and a Kentucky school district.

What were the allegations against TikTok?

The state of Alabama had argued that TikTok's endless stream of videos makes it the most addictive of social media platforms and that its algorithm specifically pushes young users toward content about violence and self harm.

The state held the app partially responsible for a teen mental health crisis and a significant increase in emergency room visits.

The lawsuit also accused TikTok of falsely claiming that it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have the app rated as 'safe for teens' on app stores.

It said that TikTok asks users to self-report their ages but also allows them to evade questions by viewing videos without creating an account.

That still earns the company data on viewing habits. Being able to scroll videos without signing in makes 'Kids Mode' an entirely useless feature, the lawsuit said.

What measures will TikTok take?

As per the settlement, TikTok has to implement a series of safety measures, including:

  • Two-hour daily limit
  • Additional parental control limiting time on platform
  • 'Productive pauses' interrupting continuous scrolling after 15 minutes, 60 minutes and 90 minutes
  • Restrict children access from 12 a.m. to 6 a.m.
  • Restrictions on push notifications during night and school hours
  • Robust measures to verify user age
  • Limits on discoverability of teen accounts by adults
  • Sending parents notifications of suspicious interactions between teen users and adults
  • Blanket ban on use of cosmetic filters by teens
  • Non-personalized feed for teens

Last month, Meta agreed to pay a massive $17 billion to 47 US states and territories in a similar case while agreeing to make changes to teens' access to its platforms, Facebook and Instagram.

It did not admit wrongdoing and conditioned $5 billion of the payout on TikTok, Snap and YouTube's adoption of the same terms. TikTok has not commented publicly about that deal.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis
entries.summary: Amid military escalation with the Iran-backed Houthis, the Saudi-backed head of Yemen's governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces.
entries.content:
Yemen

Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis

September 25, 2026

Amid military escalation with the Iran-backed Houthis, the Saudi-backed head of Yemen's governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces.

Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, on Friday called for a general mobilization in the war-torn country.

"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilization and national mobilization, to rally around their armed and security forces," al-Alimi, who is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a televised address.

The head of the governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces weeks after Yemen's government was dealt a major blow by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, allowing them to fully control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, igniting global fears about shipping through the chokepoint.

What else did Yemen's leader say?

In his address, al-Alimi also said that the objective of the mobilization is to "restore state institutions and extend sovereignty over the entire national territory," including the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since 2014.

He added that anyone who defects from the Houthis to the government will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty.

Al-Alimi addressed residents of Houthi-controlled areas, urging them to protect their children and not send them to fight alongside the Houthis.

"The state does not view you as a party to the conflict but as its people and partners," he said.

Houthis escalate conflict

For more than a decade, the Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government. Although a 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, fighting has recently flared up again amid the wider conflict involving Iran.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have intensified their missile and drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi targets in an attempt to stifle Saudi oil exports.

The Houthis accuse the kingdom of besieging Yemeni areas under their control. They attacked Riyadh for the first time in years over the weekend, marking a major escalation.

Edited by: Rana Taha

Brazil

Lula or Bolsonaro as president? Brazil gears up to vote

September 25, 2026

Brazilians go to the polls on October 4. The front-runners are multilateralist incumbent Lula da Silva and former President Jair Bolsonaro's son, Flavio, who wants to bring Brazil closer to the US and away from China.

Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva spoke in no uncertain terms at the opening of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday in New York: "Brazil does not belong in anyone's backyard," the Brazilian president said. His comment was directed at his US counterpart Donald Trump, despite Trump not being in attendance.

The US president has repeatedly interfered with Brazilian domestic politics, siding with former President Jair Messias Bolsonaro and the far-right opposition. In July, Trump imposed sanctions on a judge who found Bolsonaro guilty of attempting a coup and sentenced him to 27 years in jail. Washington only lifted the sanctions after negotiating with Lula.

Bolsonaro's eldest son Flavio is Lula's biggest challenger in the upcoming presidential election on October 4, and polls currently show the two of them to be neck and neck in a potential runoff.

The election in the world's fifth largest country is drawing a great deal of international attention. Brazil is an agricultural giant and very rich in natural resources — boasting rare earth elements, vast water resources and enormous crude oil reserves.

Brazil one of South America's last bastions of the left

Lula is the "last man standing" of the South American left, while Flavio Bolsonaro is part of an increasingly strong far-right camp. Argentina, Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Ecuador and Colombia all have governments that are sympathetic to Trump. And since January, Venezuela has been what some describe as a US protectorate.

Foreign policy hasn't played a big role in the campaign, but this election will nonetheless decide whether Brazil moves closer to Trump's US. Washington is seeking economic and military dominance in South America through the Shield of the Americas initiative, focused on combating violent cartels. After his military intervention in Venezuela, Trump is now exerting economic pressure on Mexico and Cuba. At the same time, he is trying to counter Chinese influence in the region.

For his part, Lula is an advocate of multilateralist diplomacy, wanting Brazil to engage in dialogue and trade with everybody. China has long been Brazil's most important trading partner.

Flavio Bolsonaro favors a conservative alliance with the US and other right-wing states. But for Leonardo Paz from the Brazilian Fundacao Getulio Vargas think tank, a Bolsonaro victory would not necessarily automatically mean better relations with the US. He told DW that Lula had established a largely normal relationship with Trump — both are 80 years old — despite some initial friction. The two leaders got along well, said Paz, even if Lula has not succumbed to Trump's pressure.

Paz did admit that if Bolsonaro won, the 45-year-old would be more likely to accommodate Trump, pointing out that his father Jair had made far-reaching concessions to the US when he was president. During Jair Bolsonaro's time in office from 2019 to 2023, Brazil agreed to forgo its "developing country status" in World Trade Organization negotiations in exchange for a mere promise that the US would back its bid to become a member of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Trump also said he was considering giving Brazil NATO "privileges." Neither promise came to anything.

"While relations with the US would continue as they are with Lula, it is completely unclear what a Flavio Bolsonaro presidency would mean," Rubens Ricupero, a former Brazilian diplomat and minister, told DW. "Lula has prestige in foreign policy, while Bolsonaro is completely inexperienced."

Would Brazil pull out of BRICS?

A victory for Bolsonaro would likely jeopardize Brazil's role in BRICS, the alliance that comprises Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and five other states. Bolsonaro has said that one of his first acts would be to review whether Brazil should stay in the alliance, arguing that BRICS only serves to provoke the US. He has also spoken out against China's efforts to reduce the global dominance of the US dollar.

It's hard to tell how serious such intentions are, considering the importance of economic ties between China and Brazil. Javier Milei, Argentina's current president, also engaged in harsh rhetoric against China before he came to power, but quickly adopted a more conciliatory tone once in office to not jeopardize Chinese loans.

"Political relations with China would likely cool, but I wouldn't expect any substantial changes in economic and commercial relations," predicted Ricupero in case of a Bolsonaro victory.

Paz agreed that Flavio Bolsonaro was unlikely to take an extremely aggressive stance toward China in case of victory. He explained that, like Milei, Jair Bolsonaro had engaged in some sharp rhetoric against Beijing at the beginning of his term but had quickly softened his tone, given the fact that Brazil's agricultural sector in particular is so dependent on China.

Paz pointed out that the Bolsonaro family enjoyed most support in Brazil's rural regions, which made good money with China. "The unknown factor with Flavio Bolsonaro is how much pressure the US would exert so that Brazil distanced itself from China and to what extent he would yield to the pressure," said Paz.

Brazil not likely to become major world player

Paz said that despite possessing enormous natural resources that are important to the global economy, Brazil would likely remain a minor player on the world stage as it had neither the economic strength to provide financial aid to other countries nor the military strength to help resolve conflicts. "This severely limits Brazil's ability to act," he said.

But Brazil could continue to be a major protagonist in the Global South, he said, as it is under Lula. "This is particularly evident in the international debate on global governance, in which Brazil raises issues such as new trading conditions, climate policy and development," he said.

Ricupero said Lula carried particular weight in foreign policy, especially regarding the environment and climate change. "His commitment to addressing ecological challenges was clear from his choice of [leading environmentalist] Marina Silva as environment minister," he said.

The former diplomat said he feared Flavio Bolsonaro would repeat the mistakes of his father, and this was one of the reasons the election was drawing such attention from around the world. He pointed out that Brazil had become more isolated after Jair Bolsonaro dismantled major environmental policies, adding that relations with the European Union had particularly suffered and negotiations on a trade agreement between Mercosur and the bloc had been put on hold. The deal was finally signed early this year.

This article was originally written in German.
